name: Victor Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. Tell me about your factory shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a fabric-cutting machine at a small upholstery factory. I lay out rolls, line up the pattern and check the first cut before a stack goes to the sewing room. I came to this line recently after years of store work, so I am still one of the junior operators even at 58. I left after secondary school and my present machine wage is near the lower end.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household situation, and how do you handle technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Esi works part-time in a laundry. Our children are grown and live away; we rent our flat and have only about three weeks of expenses saved. There are few other factories close enough for me to reach, so I need this shift. I do not use AI tools and prefer the cutting sheet I know. I learn a new setting slowly by doing it beside the experienced cutter, not by pressing through a menu alone. We would like to stop full shifts one day, but we have not priced that properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the cutting room that a quiet AI future leaves the machine and pattern checks in our hands. If the office prints orders faster, I still need the right fabric laid out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Esi and I can pay our rent if our present hours continue. Three weeks saved is not enough for a serious interruption, and I am still learning the cutting machine. I would stay close to the older cutter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep laying out the fabric and ask the senior cutter to check my first stack. I would follow the written pattern sheet rather than try an AI answer I cannot verify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about money even in this calm picture. The machine itself is familiar enough when the senior cutter is beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does a wrong cut begin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the edge of the roll, where the fabric is not lying flat. I know one crooked first cut can spoil the whole upholstery stack. I stop and smooth it before starting the blade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI pattern guide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask someone to demonstrate it on a spare roll and compare the marks with our written sheet. I have never used an AI tool. I would not risk customer fabric to learn it alone.

say: I would **keep** written pattern checks as office orders speed up.
A **person** still needs to flatten fabric before cutting.
think: **Present** wages meet rent only if both sets of hours hold.
**Three** weeks saved and junior status leave little margin.
do: **Keep** cutting fabric while a senior cutter checks the first stack.
**Use** the written pattern sheet for settings.
feel: **Uneasy** about thin savings despite familiar machine work.
S0.quote: I know one crooked first cut can spoil the whole upholstery stack.
fieldNote: **Victor** is a junior upholstery-fabric cutter who learned the machine after earlier store work.
He **has** secondary schooling, lower operator pay and roughly three weeks of expenses saved with part-time working wife Esi.
He **never** uses AI and wants demonstrated, written and supervised machine settings.

steps.text: Keep cutting fabric with senior first-stack checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman which office orders are changing first and whether a robot cutter is actually planned later. People should not lose hours on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can still see a crooked fabric edge, but an automatic loader could let fewer people work a shift. As a newer cutter, I would be near the front of any hours cut. Three weeks saved would go before I found another local job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to watch a guarded full-roll trial before anyone changes my cutter station. I would ask the foreman for a written hours plan and keep the present shift. If a local manual cutting vacancy is posted, I would apply only if the net wage after travel and the shift cover our rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing hours. I would not touch a robot blade just because I have watched it move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you operate the new cutter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid supervised place with a trainer showing guard stops and isolation, followed by time to practise on scrap fabric. Watching is not instruction. I would have to be offered that place before I could take responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for the hours plan now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the foreman intends one person to tend two cutters, I need to know whose hours change. My wife Esi and I cannot cover rent with guesses. A written rota lets us calculate what we can afford.

say: I would **ask** for the sequence of office and cutter changes.
I would **request** written hours before any station is removed.
think: A **later** automatic loader may reduce my junior fabric-cutting shifts.
**Three** weeks saved cannot cover a long job search.
do: **Request** a guarded full-roll demonstration and written hours plan.
**Keep** the existing cutting shift while terms are uncertain.
**Apply** for posted local cutting work only if net pay and shift cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and unwilling to operate a robot without instruction.
S1.quote: I would not touch a robot blade just because I have watched it move.
fieldNote: **Victor** would observe a robot cutter rather than claim to have learned it.
**Actual** operation needs an offered paid supervised place with guard, isolation and scrap-fabric practice.
A **separate** local job application needs a real posting and net pay and hours sufficient for rent.

steps.text: Request guarded full-roll trial and written cutting-hours plan
Apply for posted local cutting vacancy only if net pay and shift cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shop that AGI changing orders in 2028 is earlier than capable robots laying and cutting fabric around 2031. We need a written notice period if the cutting shifts will end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our small cutting crew to be reduced sharply once robots can spread, cut and stack the fabric. I will be 63 then, with three weeks saved and few local plants to ask. Esi’s part-time laundry wages would not cover the rent alone, and I would be up at night wondering where we would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop the planned replacement sofa and put rent, utilities and food on one page. I would ask the landlord about payment arrangements before missing rent and ask the shop for written severance terms. I would apply for posted local warehouse checking work only if paid safety instruction is provided and the net wage, travel and hours meet our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can count fabric scraps, but that will not pay rent when robots take my cutting hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children cover the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put that on them. They have their own households and I do not know what they could offer. I would ask about real arrangements before treating family help as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any warehouse job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If it needs lifting equipment, I would require paid safety training and a real posted wage. Travel costs matter when the pay is low. I cannot jump from a cutting shift into an unpaid promise.

say: I would **ask** for written notice before hands-on cutting robots around 2031.
**Order** software changes in 2028 come earlier than physical fabric work.
think: I **expect** a sharp loss of cutting hours at 63.
**Three** weeks saved and part-time partner pay cannot carry rent.
do: **Cancel** the planned sofa and list essential bills.
**Ask** landlord about rent arrangements and shop for written severance.
**Apply** for posted warehouse checking only with paid safety training and bill-covering net pay and hours.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless over rent.
S2.quote: I can count fabric scraps, but that will not pay rent when robots take my cutting hours.
fieldNote: **Victor** expects capable robots to threaten cutting shifts around 2031, three years after AGI changes orders.
His **tiny** reserve, low wages and scarce local factories leave little protection at age 63.
**Any** warehouse application needs an actual posting, paid safety training and enough net income after travel.

steps.text: Cancel planned replacement sofa and list essential bills
Ask landlord about payment arrangements before missed rent
Ask shop for written severance terms
Apply for posted warehouse job only with paid safety training bill-covering net wage and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the foreman five years is enough to show us a real training place before robots cut fabric around 2034. AGI changes orders in 2031, but our blade work comes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 near that robot date. I would like to reduce work eventually, but three weeks saved is no way to assume retirement. I am still learning this cutter and would need proper practical instruction for a robot cell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would accept a recognised machine-inspection course only if the shop offers a funded place on paid shifts, with supervised guard and lockout practice I can manage around my work hours. After completing it, I would apply for a posted local inspection job only if its net pay after travel meets rent and bills. If no safe paid place comes, I would stay on the cutter and search posted nearby packing jobs whose wage and shifts work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about having to retrain while I still need every wage week. Five years will help only if a place and a job really open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful lesson look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer would show me how to stop the blade, lock it and test that it cannot start. I would practise with the trainer beside me on paid time. I would not call a paper test enough to operate a robot cutter safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire instead of changing jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Esi and I first need written figures for our expected income and rent. I would not assume a pension or stop paid shifts because of my age. If the figures fall short, I must keep looking for paid work.

say: I would **ask** for an offered funded paid practical course.
**Robots** change blade work around 2034 after 2031 AGI order changes.
think: At 66, **thin** savings do not prove I can retire.
**Robot** isolation is a skill I have not yet learned.
do: **Accept** offered funded paid recognised course only with supervised lockout and workable hours.
**Apply** after training for posted inspection job only with rent-covering net pay after travel.
If **no** paid place, seek posted packing work with sufficient wage and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about earning while learning and finding a real vacancy.
S3.quote: I would not call a paper test enough to operate a robot cutter safely.
fieldNote: **Victor** would take an offered recognised funded paid place with supervised blade isolation, not a course leaflet.
A **separate** inspection application needs a posted local job and enough net pay after travel for rent.
**Without** a safe paid place he retains his cutter wage and seeks posted packing work.

steps.text: Take offered funded paid recognised course with supervised lockout and workable hours
Apply after course for posted inspection job only with rent-covering net pay after travel
Seek posted nearby packing work if no course and wage and shifts suffice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shop that ten years gives us time to write down a proper training route and retirement costs. AGI changes orders in 2036 and capable robots take fabric handling around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 at the AGI date and 71 around the robot date. I hope to have stopped full shifts by then, but Esi and I have not proved we can pay rent without wages. Any plan for working at 71 has to be conditional on those figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request our expected retirement income and costs first. If the figures say I still need a wage, I would take an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised blade and robot isolation on hours I can attend, then apply for a posted local inspection job only if its net wage and hours cover rent and travel. Without a safe paid course I would check posted packing work with enough pay and workable shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a long date that could leave me earning at 71. I can use a longer robot warning to calculate retirement costs, but it will not put money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first retirement figure you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The amount we would actually have each month after rent and utilities, compared with what food and transport cost. I would ask for written estimates before choosing an exit date. I cannot spend a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on your children then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would welcome a visit, but their households should not be our retirement fund. If the numbers do not work, I would search for paid work I can safely do. We need our own plan.

say: I would **ask** for retirement figures and a paid training route.
2036 **order** AI comes before hands-on robots around 2039.
think: At 68 in 2036 I **may** have left full shifts if income allows.
At 71 **near** 2039 continued factory work depends on actual costs.
do: **Request** written retirement income and household cost estimates.
Take **offered paid training** only if retirement figures show wages are still needed, with funding, safe practice and attendable hours.
Apply after **course** for posted local inspection only if net wage and hours cover rent and travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about uncertain retirement income and possible work at 71.
S4.quote: I can use a longer robot warning to calculate retirement costs, but it will not put money in the bank.
fieldNote: **Victor** does not assume any pension amount or promise employment after 2036.
If he **still** needs wages, training requires an offered funded paid safe place on attendable hours.
A **posted** inspection job must cover rent and travel; absent training, he checks viable posted packing work.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures
Take offered funded paid safe course on attendable hours only if figures show wages needed
Apply after course for posted inspection work with net pay and hours covering rent and travel
Check posted packing work if no safe course and pay and shifts suffice

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because robots could cut my fabric-machine shifts around 2031 when I am 63, with almost no savings or nearby jobs. A paid safe course and a real posted job that covers rent would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I am not against a machine that cuts straight. I need someone to show me how to stop the fabric cutter safely before anyone asks me to run it. I know one crooked first cut can spoil the whole upholstery stack.

headlineQuote: I need someone to show me how to stop the fabric cutter safely before anyone asks me to run it.
portrait: **Victor** Okafor, 58, is a junior upholstery-fabric cutter with secondary schooling and lower operator pay.
He and **part-time** laundry worker wife Esi rent a flat, have grown children and about three weeks saved.
He **never** uses AI tools and learns machine settings slowly with an experienced cutter beside him.
**Few** similar local jobs and no assured retirement income make his future cutting hours a serious concern.
He would **take** only offered funded paid safe training and seek a posted job with enough net pay for rent.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots could cut his fabric-machine shifts around 2031 with only three weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** funded paid supervised safety training and posted local work with net wages covering rent and travel.
